b) consider whether in the context of the requirements of the applicable financial reporting framework and the 
results of procedures performed: 
i. 
The terminology used in the financial statements including the title of each financial statement is 
appropriate; 
ii. The financial statements adequately disclose the significant accounting policies selected and applied; 
iii. The accounting policies selected and applied are consistent with the applicable financial reporting 
framework and are appropriate; 
iv. Accounting estimates made by management appear reasonable; 
v. 
The information presented in the financial statements appears relevant, reliable, comparable, and 
understandable; and 
vi. The financial statements provide adequate disclosures.  
Unmodified Conclusion 
The practitioner shall express an unmodified conclusion in the practitioner's report on the financial statements 
as a whole when the practitioner has obtained limited assurance to be able to conclude that nothing has come to 
the practitioner's attention that causes the practitioner to believe that the financial statements are not prepared, 
in all material respects, in accordance with the applicable financial reporting framework. 
Modified Conclusion 
The practitioner shall express a modified conclusion in the practitioner's report on the financial statements as a 
whole when: 
a) The practitioner determines, that the financial statements are materially misstated; or 
b) The practitioner is unable to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence. 
When the practitioner modifies the conclusion expressed on the financial statements, the practitioner shall: 
a) use the heading "Qualified Conclusion," "Adverse Conclusion" or "Disclaimer of Conclusion," as 
appropriate, for the conclusion paragraph in the practitioner's report; and 
b) provide a description of the matter giving rise to the modification. 
Financial statements are materially misstated 
If the practitioner determines that the financial statements are materially misstated, the practitioner shall 
express: 
a) A qualified conclusion, when the practitioner concludes that the effects of the matter(s) giving rise to the 
modification are material, but not pervasive to the financial statements; or 
b) An adverse conclusion, when the effects of the matter(s) giving rise to the modification are both material 
and pervasive to the financial statements. 
In the basis for conclusion paragraph, in relation to material misstatements that give rise to either a qualified 
conclusion or an adverse conclusion, the practitioner shall describe and quantify the financial effects of the 
misstatement if the material misstatement relates to specific accounts in the financial statements (including 
quantitative disclosures), unless impracticable, in which case the practitioner shall also explain: 
i. 
how disclosures are misstated; or 
ii. the nature of omitted information.

Inability to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence 
If the practitioner is unable to form a conclusion on the financial statements due to inability to obtain sufficient 
appropriate evidence the practitioner shall: 
a) Express a qualified conclusion if the practitioner concludes that the possible effects on the financial 
statements of undetected misstatements, if any, could be material but not pervasive; or 
b) Disclaim a conclusion if the practitioner concludes that the possible effects on the financial statements of 
undetected misstatements, if any, could be both material and pervasive. 
The practitioner shall disclaim a conclusion on the financial statements, or withdraw from the engagement, if: 
a) The practitioner concludes that there is sufficient doubt about the integrity of management; or 
b) Management does not provide the representations that are the preconditions for accepting an engagement.

the practitioner conclusion on the financial statements as a whole

2 INTRODUCTION TO THE ASSURANCE ENGAGEMENTS  
2.1 Definition of assurance 
‘Assurance’ means confidence. In an assurance engagement, an ‘assurance firm’ is engaged by one party to give 
an opinion on a piece of information that has been prepared by another party. The opinion is an expression of 
assurance about the information that has been reviewed. It gives assurance to the party that hired the assurance 
firm that the information can be relied on. 
As per the study text area covered till this point, what we have learned is that, assurance can be provided by: 
• 
audit: this may be external audit, internal audit or a combination of the two 
• 
review. 
A statutory audit is one form of assurance. Without assurance from the auditors, the shareholders may not accept 
that the information provided by the financial statements is sufficiently accurate and reliable. The statutory audit 
provides assurance as to the quality of the information. 
The provision of this assurance should add credibility to the information in the financial statements, making the 
information more reliable and therefore more useful to the user. 
However, there are differing levels or degrees of assurance. Some assurances are more reliable than others.  
2.2 Levels of assurance  
The degree of assurance that can be provided about the reliability of the financial statements of a company will 
depend on:  
• 
the amount of work performed in carrying out the assurance process, and  
• 
the results of that work.  
The resulting assurance falls into one of two categories: 
• 
Reasonable Assurance – A high (but not absolute) level of assurance provided by the practitioner’s 
conclusion expressed in a positive form. E.g. “In our opinion the accounts are true and fair”. The objective of 
a statutory audit is to provide reasonable assurance. 
• 
Limited Assurance – A moderate level of assurance provided by the practitioner’s conclusion expressed in 
a negative form. E.g. “Based on our review, nothing has come to our attention that causes us to believe that 
the accompanying financial statements do not give a true and fair view”. The objective of a review engagement 
is often to provide limited assurance. 
Assurance provided by audit  
An audit provides a high, but not absolute, level of assurance that the audited information is free from any 
material misstatement. This is often referred to as reasonable assurance. 
The reason why auditor is not expected to provide absolute assurance is that there are inherent limitations of an 
audit, which result in most of the audit evidence on which the auditor draws conclusions and bases the auditor’s 
opinion being persuasive rather than conclusive. The inherent limitations of an audit are discussed later in this 
chapter. 
Assurance provided by review 
A review in contrast to ‘reasonable’ level of assurance provided by an audit, a review into an aspect of the 
financial statements would provide only a moderate level of assurance that the information under review is free 
of material misstatement. The resulting opinion is usually (although not always) expressed in the form of 
negative assurance.

Negative assurance is an opinion that nothing is obviously wrong: in other words, ‘nothing has come to our 
attention to suggest that the information is misstated’. 
A review does not provide the same amount of assurance as an audit. An external audit provides positive 
assurance that, in the opinion of the auditors, the financial statements do present fairly the financial position 
and performance of the company. 
The higher level of assurance provided by an audit will enhance the credibility provided by the assurance 
process, but the audit work is likely to be:  
• 
more time-consuming than a review, and so 
• 
costlier than a review. 
2.3 Elements of an assurance engagement  
 Definition: Assurance engagement 
An engagement in which a practitioner aims to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence in order to express a 
conclusion designed to enhance the degree of confidence of the intended users other than the responsible party 
about the subject matter information (that is, the outcome of the measurement or evaluation of an underlying 
subject matter against criteria). 
An assurance engagement performed by a practitioner will consists of the following five elements: 
• 
A three party relationship: 
- 
Practitioner – the individual providing professional services that will review the subject matter and 
provide the assurance. E.g. the audit firm in a statutory audit 
- 
Responsible party – the person(s) responsible for the subject matter. E.g. the Directors are responsible 
for preparing the financial statements to be audited 
- 
Intended users – the person(s) or class of persons for whom the practitioner prepares the assurance 
report. E.g. the shareholders in a statutory audit 
• 
Subject matter: This is the data such as the financial statements that have been prepared by the responsible 
party for the practitioner to evaluate. Another example might be a cash flow forecast to be reviewed by the 
practitioner. 
• 
Suitable criteria: This can be thought of as ‘the rules’ against which the subject matter is evaluated in order 
to reach an opinion. In a statutory audit this would be the applicable reporting framework (e.g. IFRS and 
company law). 
• 
Evidence: Information used by the practitioner in arriving at the conclusion on which their opinion is based. 
This must be sufficient (enough) and appropriate (relevant). 
• 
Assurance Report: The report (normally written) containing the practitioner’s opinion. This is issued to the 
intended user following the collection of evidence.

responsible party and intended users.  
ii. Subject matter: This is the data such as the financial statements that have been prepared by the responsible 
party for the practitioner to evaluate.  
iii. Evidence: Information used by the practitioner in arriving at the conclusion on which their opinion is based. 
This must be sufficient and appropriate.  
iv. Assurance Report: The report containing the practitioner’s opinion. This is issued to the intended user(s) 
following the collection of evidence.

2.4 Objectives of an assurance engagement  
The primary objective of an assurance engagement is to enhance the degree of confidence of the intended 
users in the subject matter information. The practitioner achieves this by gathering sufficient appropriate 
evidence and expressing a written conclusion about the subject matter's conformity with identified criteria.  
Beyond this overall purpose, specific assurance engagements may have more tailored objectives. For instance, 
an assurance engagement could be designed to conclude on the effectiveness of internal controls, compliance 
with laws or regulations, sustainability metrics, or other subject matters. In each case, however, the common 
objective is to have a qualified independent practitioner evaluate the subject matter against suitable criteria and 
provide a conclusion (often in the form of an opinion or report) that lends credibility to the subject matter 
information.  
2.5  Phases of an Assurance Engagement 
Assurance engagements, much like audits, typically progress through a series of phases or stages. Each phase has 
specific activities and objectives, ensuring a systematic approach to achieving the engagement’s overall goal. 
While the exact terminology may vary, we can summarize the phases as follows: 
Phase 
Description 
1. Acceptance and 
Continuance 
Practitioner ensures all preconditions are met (e.g., subject matter, criteria, 
evidence, independence). If any are missing, the engagement is declined. 
2. Planning 
An overall strategy and detailed plan are developed, assessing risks and 
defining materiality to guide resource allocation and procedures. 
3. Execution (Evidence 
Gathering) 
Assurance procedures (e.g., inspections, confirmations, analytics) are 
carried out, with updates to the plan as needed and professional scepticism 
maintained. 
4. Evaluation and Conclusion 
Evidence is evaluated against criteria, considering materiality and 
qualitative factors. Inconsistencies are resolved before forming a conclusion. 
5. Reporting 
An assurance report is issued, detailing scope, responsibilities, and the 
conclusion. It clearly distinguishes the engagement from non-assurance 
ones. 
2.6  Types of Assurance Engagements 
The IAASB’s assurance framework recognises several types or categories of assurance engagements, which can 
be distinguished by their subject matters, their structure, or the standards under which they are performed. Here 
we discuss a few ways to classify assurance engagements: 
• 
Attestation Engagement (Assertion-Based) 
In this type, the responsible party (e.g., management) evaluates the subject matter and provides subject 
matter information (like financial statements). 
The practitioner’s role is to assess and attest whether this information is reliable. 
An audit is a common example: management prepares the statements, and the auditor expresses an opinion 
on them. The report refers to the assertion made by the responsible party. 
• 
Direct Engagement (Direct Reporting) 
Here, the practitioner directly evaluates the subject matter without a prior assertion from management. 
They both measure and report the outcome (e.g., effectiveness of internal controls). The report includes the 
subject matter information and the conclusion. This type is often used in non-financial assurance like 
compliance audits.

2.7 Non-Assurance Engagements: 
The IAASB clearly distinguishes assurance engagements from other professional services where no assurance is 
expressed. While assurance engagements aim to provide a conclusion that enhances the confidence of users 
(such as audits and reviews), many services provided by accountants fall under non-assurance engagements, 
which include compilation, valuation, and recruitment services. These services do not meet the criteria for 
assurance under the IAASB framework and are often classified as advisory, consulting, or related services. 
• 
Preparing Accounting Records and Financial Statements 
This involves assisting management in compiling financial information such as maintaining ledgers, posting 
journal entries, or drafting financial statements. Governed by ISRS 4410, this is a related service, not an 
assurance engagement. The practitioner does not provide a conclusion or opinion on the accuracy of the 
information. Instead, the client is responsible for the financial information's reliability. The compilation 
report clearly states that no assurance is provided. However, when the same firm is also the auditor, ethical 
concerns may arise due to the self-review threat. 
• 
Valuation Services 
Valuation involves estimating the worth of assets, liabilities, or businesses for example, in mergers, fair value 
accounting, or asset impairments. While it may appear similar to assurance, valuation is an expert or 
consulting service, not an assurance engagement, because it does not involve evaluating information against 
a formal set of criteria for external users. The accountant provides management with a valuation report, not 
an assurance conclusion. If, however, an accountant were to audit a fair value prepared by someone else, 
that may constitute an assurance task. Ethical and independence rules still apply if the valuation is done for 
an audit client.

• 
Recruitment Services 
Recruitment services involve helping clients hire staff—for example, screening candidates or assisting in 
executive hiring. These are clearly consulting services, not assurance engagements, as they do not involve 
verifying information or issuing a conclusion. The practitioner provides advice, not confidence to third-party 
users. However, ethical issues arise if such services are provided to audit clients, especially in hiring senior 
management, as it may create self-interest or familiarity threats. 
In conclusion, these non-assurance services differ fundamentally from assurance engagements because they 
do not include the expression of an independent conclusion intended to instil confidence in users. While 
professional standards and ethical requirements still apply, such engagements fall outside the scope of 
IAASB assurance standards. Understanding these distinctions is important for proper application of 
standards and maintaining independence in practice.

3 ASSURANCE ENGAGEMENTS - OTHER CONSIDERATIONS  
3.1  Material Misstatement: Concept and Impact on Assurance 
A material misstatement occurs when subject matter information (like financial statements or sustainability 
reports) deviates from the applicable criteria in a way that could reasonably influence user decisions. 
Misstatements can arise from errors or fraud and may be quantitative or qualitative. 
• 
Planning: Practitioners set materiality thresholds early to determine the focus areas. These thresholds 
depend on user needs and engagement context. 
• 
Risk Assessment: Includes identifying inherent and control risks in high-judgment or error-prone areas 
(e.g., revenue recognition). 
• 
Detection and Evaluation: Practitioners detect misstatements during evidence gathering. If material, they 
may extend procedures to assess full impact. 
• 
Correction and Reporting: Misstatements are discussed with management. If uncorrected and material, 
they affect the audit opinion leading to qualified or adverse opinions. 
• 
Communication: All significant misstatements, corrected or uncorrected, are communicated to 
management or governance bodies. 
3.2 Traditional Assurance Procedures 
Traditional assurance procedures include: 
• 
Inquiry:  
 
Asking informed personnel questions. 
• 
Inspection:  
 
Examining documents or assets. 
• 
Observation:  
 
Watching processes being performed. 
• 
Recalculation:   
Verifying arithmetic accuracy. 
• 
Reperformance:   
Repeating the procedures of responsible parties. 
• 
Analytical Procedures:  Studying trends, ratios and applying mathematical reasoning. 
• 
External Confirmation:  Getting independent verification from third parties. 
3.3 Automated Tools and Techniques (ATT) 
Automated Tools and Techniques (ATT) refer to the use of technology to perform assurance procedures 
traditionally done manually. The IAASB defines ATT broadly, covering everything from data analytics to AI, RPA 
(Robotic Process Automation), and even drones. 
Types and Uses of ATT 
ATT can range from basic (e.g., using Excel) to advanced tools like: 
• 
Generalized Audit Software (GAS) for sorting and analyzing entire data sets. 
• 
Data Analytics to detect anomalies and trends across full populations. 
• 
Process Mining and Risk Visualization for identifying control weaknesses or risks. 
• 
Digital Confirmations to streamline third-party evidence gathering. 
• 
RPA and AI to automate repetitive tasks or analyze contracts and transactions. 
• 
Drones for inventory observation in inaccessible locations.

3.4  Quality of evidence and its impact on conclusions 
In assurance engagements, practitioners rely on sufficient appropriate evidence, which must be both relevant 
(logically connected to the assertion) and reliable (from trustworthy sources). When evidence is consistent, 
forming a conclusion is relatively straightforward. However, when contradictory evidence arises, it can 
complicate professional judgment and decision-making. 
Contradictory evidence occurs when one piece of evidence supports a conclusion, while another suggests the 
opposite. For example, if customer confirmations agree with receivable balances but internal ledgers show 
discrepancies, the auditor cannot immediately conclude that receivables are fairly stated. Instead, they must 
investigate the inconsistency. 
Such contradictions require the practitioner to: 
• 
Weigh the reliability of each piece (e.g., external vs. internal sources). 
• 
Perform additional procedures to resolve inconsistencies. 
• 
Avoid relying on incomplete or biased evidence, even if voluminous. 
• 
Adjust the risk assessment, strategy, or conclusion if the contradiction cannot be resolved.

If unresolved, contradictory evidence may lead the practitioner to modify the opinion, expand testing, or 
withhold assurance. For example, if a lawyer’s letter discloses litigation that management denies, this indicates 
a possible misstatement or management bias, requiring deeper inquiry. 
Ultimately, conclusions must be well-reasoned and evidence-based. If multiple sources corroborate a finding, 
confidence increases. If evidence conflicts, the practitioner must either resolve the conflict or reflect the 
uncertainty in their report, ensuring that users are not misled by an overconfident conclusion. Thus, handling 
contradictory evidence is a critical test of professional scepticism and judgment in any assurance engagement. 
3.5  Connected Information 
Connected information refers to data or evidence that links various elements of the subject matter being 
examined. In assurance engagements, this interconnectedness helps practitioners form a more complete, 
coherent understanding of the entity’s operations, risks, and controls. 
When information from different sources (e.g., financial, operational, regulatory) aligns, it enhances the 
reliability and persuasiveness of evidence. For example, if sales data, bank deposits, and tax filings all support 
recorded revenue, the assurance gained is stronger. 
Conversely, inconsistencies or gaps in connected information can signal errors, fraud, or control weaknesses, 
prompting further investigation. For instance, if payroll records and HR reports do not reconcile, it may suggest 
fictitious employees or poor controls. 
Connected information also aids in risk assessment, helping practitioners identify unusual patterns or 
anomalies across systems. It enables cross-validation of evidence and supports more informed judgments and 
conclusions. 
Using connected information helps the practitioner see the full picture and understand how different parts of the 
business relate to each other. This leads to better, more accurate assurance and gives more confidence in the 
assurance report. 
3.6  Sufficiency, Appropriateness, and Documentation 
In an assurance engagement, the auditor must obtain and document sufficient appropriate evidence to support 
their conclusion. This means the evidence must be enough in quantity (sufficiency) and high in quality 
(appropriateness, which includes relevance and reliability). 
To assess whether this has been achieved, the practitioner considers: 
• 
Coverage: Have all significant areas, risks, and assertions been addressed through relevant procedures? 
• 
Reliability: Has the evidence come from dependable sources (e.g., third parties, direct observation, or 
recalculation)? 
• 
Relevance: Does the evidence directly relate to the specific assertion or subject matter? 
• 
Consistency: Does the evidence from various procedures and sources support the same conclusion, or are 
there contradictions that require further work? 
In an assurance engagement, proper documentation is much critical. The practitioner must clearly record: 
• 
What procedures were performed 
• 
What evidence was obtained 
• 
How that evidence supports the conclusion 
The documentation should be clear and complete so that another experienced assurance practitioner could 
understand the nature, timing, and extent of the procedures, and how the evidence led to the conclusion. If 
documentation is lacking or unclear, it may appear that the assurance conclusion is not well supported, even if 
sufficient appropriate evidence was actually gathered. Therefore, thorough documentation is just as important 
as obtaining the evidence itself in delivering a credible assurance engagement

4 SUSTAINABILITY ASSURANCE IN AUDIT CONTEXT 
4.1 Requirements of Sustainability Reporting in an Audit Context 
Requirements of Sustainability Reporting in an Audit Context 
Sustainability reporting discloses an organization’s environmental, social, and governance (ESG) performance, 
using frameworks such as IFRS Sustainability Disclosure Standards (S1 & S2) and Global Reporting Initiative 
(GRI) Standards. These frameworks ensure transparency, comparability, and completeness, forming the 
foundation for audit and assurance engagements. 
For sustainability information to be assured, certain preconditions must be met: 
• 
Use of recognised reporting frameworks (GRI, IFRS S1/S2, SASB). 
• 
Disclosure of material ESG matters that significantly impact stakeholders. 
• 
Compliance with regulatory requirements (e.g., Code of Corporate Governance). 
Auditors assess sustainability information against suitable criteria, ensuring it is verifiable, measurable, and 
reliable. Like financial audits, sustainability reporting requires proper documentation to support assurance 
engagements.

4.2 Disclosures in Assurance of Sustainability Reporting

disclosures include:

• 
Level of assurance (reasonable or limited). 
• 
Scope of work and procedures performed. 
• 
Responsibilities of management and the assurance provider.

independence. Any limitations (e.g., exclusions of certain data) must be disclosed to ensure transparency.

4.3  Ethical Considerations for Assurance of Sustainability Reporting 
The International Ethics Standards for Sustainability Assurance (IESSA) introduces the need for ethical 
consideration in such engagements by following words: 
“It is of public interest that sustainability assurance practitioners act ethically in order to maintain public trust and 
confidence in sustainability information that is subject to assurance. High-quality ethics and independence 
standards alongside other reporting and assurance standards will help investors, customers, employees and other 
users of sustainability information to confidently rely on such information in their decision-making (5100.1)” 
“Sustainability assurance practitioners are expected to have relevant knowledge, skills and experience to perform 
sustainability assurance engagements and have appropriate training to ensure their assurance skills are continually 
up to date with relevant developments (5100.1a)” 
The fundamental principles are: 
a) Integrity – to be straightforward and honest in all professional and business relationships. 
b) Objectivity – to not allow bias, conflict of interest or undue influence of others to override professional or 
business judgments. 
c) Professional Competence and Due Care – to: 
- 
Attain and maintain professional knowledge and skill at the level required to ensure that a sustainability 
assurance client receives competent professional service, based on current technical and professional 
standards and relevant legislation; and 
- 
Act diligently and in accordance with applicable technical and professional standards. 
d) Confidentiality – to respect the confidentiality of information acquired as a result of professional and 
business relationships. 
e) Professional Behaviour – to comply with relevant laws and regulations and avoid any conduct that the 
sustainability assurance practitioner knows or should know might discredit the sustainability assurance 
profession 
High ethical standards (e.g., IESBA Code of Ethics) protect public trust in sustainability reporting.

4.4 Examples of Sustainability Reporting in an Audit Context 
1. Framework-Based Reporting and Assurance 
Company A publishes a sustainability report using GRI Standards, covering carbon emissions, energy usage,

using ISAE 3000/ISSA 5000. The assurance statement confirms no material misstatements, reinforcing 
stakeholder trust. 
2. Mandatory Sustainability Reporting with Audit Oversight

review sustainability disclosures for material inconsistencies under ISA 720 (Other Information). 
Additionally, greenhouse gas emissions are independently verified under ISO 14064 standards, ensuring 
compliance and strengthening investor confidence. 
3. Ethical Independence in Assurance Services 
Company C, a tech firm, seeks sustainability assurance after hiring a consultancy to develop its ESG data 
systems. Its audit firm identifies a self-review threat and assigns a separate assurance team to maintain 
independence. The assurance report follows IESBA’s Code of Ethics, explicitly confirming independence and 
ethical compliance. 
4. Reasonable Assurance on Key ESG Metrics 
Company D requires reasonable assurance on workplace safety and GHG emissions, key ESG metrics for 
investors and regulators. The assurance provider conducts in-depth testing (inspections, data verification,

5. Public Accountability in Sustainability Assurance 
Company E, a state-owned enterprise, must report national sustainability commitments (e.g., emissions 
reduction). An independent auditor provides reasonable assurance, addressing the report to management, 
regulators, and public stakeholders. This ensures full transparency and reinforces public trust.

5 SUSTAINABILITY ASSURANCE ENGAGEMENTS (ISSA 5000) 
5.1  Introduction to Sustainability Assurance Engagements  
The scope of the assurance engagement may extend to all of the sustainability information to be reported by the 
entity or only part of that information. For example, some jurisdictions may require the entirety of the 
sustainability information to be reported in accordance with an established framework to be subject to 
assurance. However, in certain jurisdictions, law or regulation may require that only climate-related disclosures 
in an entity’s sustainability information be subject to assurance. The reporting requirements of this ISSA require 
the practitioner to identify or describe the information that is subject to the assurance engagement 
Sustainability assurance engagements independently evaluate ESG disclosures, ensuring transparency, 
reliability, and accountability. These engagements align sustainability assurance with financial audits, following 
standards like ISAE 3000 and IAASB’s ISSA 5000. 
Levels of Assurance 
• 
Limited assurance – Moderate confidence (e.g. no evidence of misstatements found). 
• 
Reasonable assurance – Higher confidence (e.g. ESG information is fairly stated). 
IAASB ISSA 5000 provides a global framework for sustainability assurance, ensuring consistent, high-quality 
engagements across industries. 
 5.2  Objectives of Sustainability Assurance Engagements 
Sustainability information is reported in accordance with the criteria. This ISSA requires the practitioner to 
evaluate whether the criteria that the practitioner expects to be applied in the preparation of the sustainability 
information are suitable for the engagement circumstances. In the absence of indications to the contrary, 
framework criteria that are embodied in law or regulation or are established by authorized or recognised 
organizations that follow a transparent due process are presumed to be suitable 
The objectives of the practitioner are to:  
• 
obtain either reasonable assurance or limited assurance, as appropriate, about whether the sustainability 
information is free from material misstatement  
• 
express a conclusion on the sustainability information through a written report that conveys a reasonable 
assurance or a limited assurance conclusion, as applicable, and describes the basis for the conclusion  
• 
communicate further as required by this ISSA and any other relevant ISSA. 
In all cases when reasonable assurance or limited assurance, as applicable, cannot be obtained and a qualified 
conclusion in the practitioner’s assurance report is insufficient in the circumstances for purposes of reporting to 
the intended users, this ISSA requires the practitioner to disclaim a conclusion or withdraw from the 
engagement, where withdrawal is possible under applicable law or regulation.

renewable energy goals. An independent assurance provider is engaged to verify whether the company met 
its agreed sustainability targets. 
Key Assurance Elements: 
• 
Subject Matter: Reported renewable energy usage percentage. 
• 
Criteria: Industry standards & bond agreement definitions of renewable energy. 
• 
Evidence Gathering: Energy purchase records, contract verifications, supplier certifications. 
• 
Assurance Level: Reasonable assurance due to financial implications. 
• 
Outcome: The assurance statement, addressed to both management and bondholders, confirms 
whether Green Energy met its target, impacting the interest rate paid on the bond. 
4. Community & NGO Assurance on Environmental and Social Impact 
Company: ABC Mining 
Scenario: Due to community concerns over its environmental and social impact, ABC Mining agrees with 
NGOs to undergo independent sustainability assurance, ensuring transparency in land restoration and 
community engagement claims. 
Key Assurance Elements: 
• 
Subject Matter: Sustainability report sections on land rehabilitation, water quality, and community 
grievance resolution. 
• 
Criteria: Local environmental laws, voluntary sustainability frameworks, and company commitments. 
• 
Evidence Gathering: Field inspections, laboratory water quality tests, community feedback analysis. 
• 
Assurance Level: Limited assurance, with an NGO-involved review process. 
• 
Outcome: The assurance report, made public, builds trust between ABC Mining, NGOs, and local 
communities, ensuring sustainability claims are independently verified.
